title: ATAR (Australian Tertiary Admission Rank)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public Australian senior secondary curriculum. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A council newsletter states that nine out of ten local families already support the new bike path and that it is time the holdouts caught up. Which persuasive technique is the writer mainly using?
options: Appealing to the reader's fear of receiving a fine
Asking a rhetorical question to create doubt in the reader
Citing majority support to pressure the reader into conformity
Establishing the writer's personal authority as an elected official
items.explanation: The statistic about majority support combined with the pressure on holdouts is the bandwagon or social-proof technique. No fine is threatened, no question is asked, and the writer claims no personal authority.

items.stem: In the line the harbour stitched the dark with light, what does the metaphor of stitching most effectively suggest about the lighthouse beams?
options: The beams were weak and faded almost immediately
The beams repeatedly crossed and mended the night like needlework
The harbour was closed to shipping for the whole night
The lighthouse keeper was repairing the lamp by hand
items.explanation: Stitching is a needlework action, so the metaphor pictures the beams crossing and re-crossing to weave the darkness together. The other readings take the image literally or add details the line never mentions.

items.stem: A novelist writes that the classroom smelt of chalk dust, warm vinyl and yesterday's rain. What is the main effect of this detail on the reader?
options: It anchors the scene in smell so the setting feels lived-in and real
It tells the reader that the weather is about to change
It establishes that the students are afraid of the teacher
It signals that the novel is set deep in the distant past
items.explanation: Naming three specific smells layers sensory detail that places the reader inside the room, making the setting feel particular and believable. Nothing in the sentence forecasts weather, implies fear, or dates the novel.

items.stem: A theatre reviewer writes that the production held her spellbound for both of its hours, apart from the few minutes near the end when she began counting the ceiling panels. What tone does the reviewer convey?
options: Ironic, because counting ceiling panels shows boredom rather than spellbinding
Sincere admiration for the actors' powerful concentration
Hostility, because the reviewer wants the production shut down
Uncertainty, because the reviewer cannot remember the play
items.explanation: Praising the performance while admitting to counting ceiling panels gives the praise a mock quality, so the tone is quietly ironic rather than admiring. There is no abuse and no confusion about what was seen.

items.stem: A novel opens with the sentence nobody in the town knew what I kept in the shed, and I meant to keep it that way. What does this first-person narration establish for the reader?
options: An objective, documentary account written by an outsider
A flashback narrated in later years by a family historian
An all-knowing narrator able to describe every character's thoughts
A narrator who holds private knowledge the other characters lack
items.explanation: The pronoun I combined with meant to keep it that way shows the speaker guards information the townspeople do not have, creating a private and possibly unreliable voice. The passage is subjective rather than objective or all-knowing.

items.stem: A student argues that the school day should begin later. She first summarises the objection that a later start would inconvenience working parents, then answers it by citing bus timetables that already run later. What is the effect of presenting the objection first?
options: It avoids the issue by changing the subject to public transport
It shows that the writer does not understand the objection
It strengthens the argument by acknowledging and then meeting a likely counterargument
It proves that parents have no valid concerns at all
items.explanation: Naming the strongest objection before rebutting it shows the writer takes opposition seriously and then neutralises it, which makes the case more persuasive. The passage does not change the subject or dismiss parents entirely.

items.stem: A speech repeats the openings we were promised safety, we were promised answers, we were promised change. Which language feature is being used?
options: Hyperbole, because the claims are deliberately exaggerated
Anaphora, because the same words open each successive clause
Onomatopoeia, because the words imitate the sound of a crowd
Euphemism, because a harsh reality is being softened
items.explanation: Repeating the identical opening across successive clauses is the definition of anaphora. Hyperbole would exaggerate, onomatopoeia would imitate a sound, and a euphemism would soften an unpleasant term.

items.stem: Throughout a short story a character repairs a broken watch that never keeps the right time. What does the watch most plausibly symbolise?
options: The character's wealth and success in business
An attempt to hold on to or repair a lost period of the past
The character's hatred of all mechanical objects
The heat of an Australian summer afternoon
items.explanation: A watch that is constantly repaired yet never tells the right time suggests a character trying and failing to recover a lost time, so the object carries emotional meaning beyond timekeeping. The other options are not developed by the story.

items.stem: A writer describes a crowd as a mob surging at the gate in one paragraph and as a gathering waiting patiently in the next. What does the shift in word choice reveal?
options: The writer is shaping the reader's attitude toward the same crowd
The two paragraphs describe two different streets
The writer has made a factual error about crowd size
The crowd has physically shrunk in number overnight
items.explanation: Changing mob surging to gathering waiting alters the connotations of identical events, steering the reader from hostility toward sympathy. The crowd itself has not moved or changed size, so no factual error is involved.

items.stem: A memoir moves from the narrator's present-day funeral back to a childhood afternoon at the beach and then returns to the funeral. What is the main effect of structuring the piece this way?
options: It removes all emotion from the funeral scene
It proves the narrator's childhood was happier than most
It links past and present so the reader understands what the loss means now
It confuses the reader about when the events took place
items.explanation: Interrupting the present with a childhood scene forces the reader to compare the two, so the death gains meaning from what came before. The structure is deliberate rather than confusing and heightens rather than removes feeling.

items.stem: A story ends with a fire station burning down while its crew are away answering a false alarm elsewhere. What kind of irony does this ending mainly create?
options: Verbal irony, because the captain says the opposite of what he means
Situational irony, because the outcome opposes the station's whole purpose
Dramatic irony, because the reader knows a fact the characters never learn
Cosmic irony, because the gods deliberately intervene in human affairs
items.explanation: A station that exists to prevent fires burning down is an outcome opposite to its purpose, which is situational irony. Verbal irony involves a speaker meaning the opposite of the words, and dramatic irony involves a knowledge gap with the audience.

items.stem: In a novel a farmer refuses free help from neighbours for years, then accepts it after a flood and works beside them for the rest of his life. Which statement best expresses an idea the novel develops?
options: Pride isolates people until hardship teaches them that interdependence is a strength
Floods are the only events that can change a person's character
Neighbours should never expect gratitude for the help they give
Farming is an unsuitable occupation for a proud person
items.explanation: The refusal of help isolates the farmer and accepting it after the flood restores him to the community, developing the idea that pride separates people until dependence on others is shown to be a strength.

items.stem: A campaign pamphlet asks do you want to pay for a stadium you will never enter rather than stating you should not pay for the stadium. What is the writer's main purpose in asking instead of telling?
options: To supply statistical evidence about stadium revenue
To apologise to readers for the cost of the project
To change the subject from sport to taxation
To make the reader reach the conclusion unaided and feel personally involved
items.explanation: A rhetorical question makes the reader supply the objection themselves, so the conclusion feels like their own and they become personally invested in the cost. The question offers no data, apology, or change of subject.

items.stem: A poet sets a stanza describing a shattered city beside a stanza describing a child laughing in a garden. What does this juxtaposition primarily achieve?
options: It proves that the two events happened on the same day
It intensifies both images by forcing innocence and destruction together
It shows that the poet cannot decide which subject to write about
It provides a break so that the poem can end quickly
items.explanation: Placing a laughing child next to a ruined city sharpens each image through contrast and makes the reader hold innocence and destruction in mind at once, which is the work of juxtaposition. Nothing here fixes a date or signals indecision.

items.stem: A council website explains composting with the sentence pop your scraps in the green bin and the worms will do the rest. Which audience is this language most likely aimed at?
options: Households, because the tone is casual and the command is friendly
Council engineers, because the tone is technical and quantitative
University biologists, because the tone is formal and specialised
Court officials, because the tone is legalistic and binding
items.explanation: The contraction, the informal verb pop and the playful finish are friendly and untechnical, which suits household readers. Engineers, biologists and legal audiences would be given precise or formal wording instead.

items.stem: Solve the quadratic equation x squared minus 5x plus 6 equals 0 for x.
options: x equals negative 2 or x equals negative 3
x equals 1 or x equals 6
x equals negative 1 or x equals negative 6
x equals 2 or x equals 3
items.explanation: The expression factorises as (x minus 2)(x minus 3) equals 0, so x is 2 or 3. The other pairs neither multiply to positive 6 nor add to negative 5 at the same time.

items.stem: For the function f of x equals the square root of x minus 4, state the domain of f in inequality form.
options: x is greater than or equal to 0
x is less than or equal to 4
x is greater than or equal to 4
x is strictly greater than 4
items.explanation: A square root is real only when the radicand is non-negative, so x minus 4 is at least 0 and x is at least 4. Values below 4 are undefined in the reals, and the strict inequality wrongly excludes 4 itself.

items.stem: If f of x equals 3x squared minus 4x plus 1, what is the gradient of the curve y equals f of x at the point where x equals 2?
items.explanation: Differentiating gives f dash x equals 6x minus 4, so at x equals 2 the gradient is 12 minus 4, which is 8. The value 5 is f of 2, the height of the curve rather than its gradient.

items.stem: Differentiate y equals the quantity 2x squared plus 3 raised to the fifth power with respect to x.
options: 5 times the quantity 2x squared plus 3 to the fourth
10x times the quantity 2x squared plus 3 to the fourth
4x times the quantity 2x squared plus 3 to the fifth
20x times the quantity 2x squared plus 3 to the fourth
items.explanation: By the chain rule multiply the outer derivative 5 times bracket to the fourth by the inner derivative 4x, giving 20x times bracket to the fourth. Omitting the inner derivative gives the second option, and the others differentiate only part of the expression.

items.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of 2x with respect to x from 0 to 3.
items.explanation: The antiderivative of 2x is x squared, so the integral is 3 squared minus 0 squared, which is 9. The other values come from evaluating the integrand at the endpoint or doubling the result instead of integrating.

items.stem: In a class 12 of the 30 students study French, and 8 of those 12 also study Japanese. If one student is chosen at random from the French students, what is the probability that the student also studies Japanese?
items.explanation: The condition that the chosen student studies French restricts the sample space to the 12 French students, and 8 of them study Japanese, so the probability is 8 divided by 12, which is 2/3. The other options use the whole class instead of the conditional group.

items.stem: A basketballer has a probability of 0.6 of scoring each independent free throw. What is the probability of scoring exactly twice in three attempts?
items.explanation: With p of 0.6, q of 0.4 and n of 3, exactly two successes gives 3 choose 2 times 0.6 squared times 0.4, which is 0.432. The value 0.216 is scoring all three, 0.288 is exactly one, and 0.648 is at least two.

items.stem: Heights of Year 12 students are normally distributed with mean 170 centimetres and standard deviation 6 centimetres. Approximately what is the probability that a randomly chosen student is taller than 176 centimetres?
items.explanation: 176 is one standard deviation above the mean, and about 68 per cent of a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean, leaving about 32 per cent outside, half of which lies above 176, giving about 0.16. The other values belong to the wrong tail or range.

items.stem: A mosquito population is estimated at 4000 and grows by 15 per cent each week. What is the estimated population after two weeks?
items.explanation: Growth compounds, so the population is 4000 times 1.15 squared, which is 5290. The value 4600 counts only one week, 5200 adds the percentages instead of multiplying, and 3025 divides rather than multiplies.

items.stem: Find all values of theta between 0 degrees and 360 degrees inclusive for which cos theta equals the square root of 3 divided by 2.
options: 30 degrees and 150 degrees
30 degrees and 330 degrees
60 degrees and 120 degrees
45 degrees and 135 degrees
items.explanation: cos of 30 degrees is root 3 over 2, and cosine is positive in the fourth quadrant as well, giving 330 degrees within the stated range. The pairs 60 and 120 degrees and 45 and 135 degrees belong to other ratios or quadrants.

items.stem: Solve the exponential equation 2 raised to the power x equals 32 for the value of x.
items.explanation: 2 raised to the fifth power is 32, so x equals 5, which is also log base 2 of 32. The other values give 2 to the sixteenth, 2 to the sixty-fourth and 2 to the tenth, none of which equal 32.

items.stem: A ball is dropped from 8 metres and after each bounce reaches half its previous height. What is the total vertical distance travelled by the ball from the first drop until it comes to rest?
options: 16 metres
8 metres
32 metres
24 metres
items.explanation: The ball falls 8 metres, then rises and falls 4 metres, then 2 metres and so on, giving 8 plus 2 times the geometric series 4 plus 2 plus 1. That series sums to 8, so the total is 8 plus 16, which is 24 metres. The other options count only part of the journey.

items.stem: Given matrix A with rows 1 2 and 3 4, and matrix B with rows 0 1 and 1 0, what is the entry in row 1 column 2 of the product AB?
items.explanation: The row 1 column 2 entry is the first row of A times the second column of B, which is 1 times 1 plus 2 times 0, giving 1. The values 2, 4 and 3 are the other three entries of the same product matrix.

items.stem: A data set of ten values has a median and a mean calculated, and then one extreme outlier is added. Which statement best describes the likely effect of the outlier?
options: Both the mean and the median increase by exactly the same amount
Neither the mean nor the median changes at all
The mean is pulled toward the outlier while the median changes little
The median increases while the mean is completely unaffected
items.explanation: The mean uses every value, so a single extreme outlier drags it toward that value, while the median depends only on the middle position and is barely moved. This robustness is why medians are preferred for skewed data.

items.stem: A rectangle has a fixed perimeter of 40 centimetres. Which dimensions give the rectangle the maximum possible area?
options: 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres, giving 100 square centimetres
5 centimetres by 15 centimetres, giving 75 square centimetres
2 centimetres by 18 centimetres, giving 36 square centimetres
20 centimetres by 20 centimetres, giving 400 square centimetres
items.explanation: For a fixed perimeter the area is greatest when the rectangle is a square, so the sides are 10 centimetres and the area is 100 square centimetres. A 20 by 20 square would need an 80 centimetre perimeter, and the other rectangles enclose less area.

items.stem: A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 metres per second squared for 4.0 seconds. What is the cyclist's final velocity?
options: 2.5 metres per second
4.0 metres per second
20 metres per second
10 metres per second
items.explanation: Using v equals u plus a t with a starting velocity of zero gives 2.5 times 4.0, which is 10 metres per second. The other options quote the acceleration, the time, or the distance travelled of 20 metres rather than the final velocity.

items.stem: A 1200 kilogram car accelerates at 1.5 metres per second squared along a level road. What net force acts on the car?
options: 800 newtons
18000 newtons
1800 newtons
1200 newtons
items.explanation: Newton's second law gives F equals m a, so 1200 times 1.5 is 1800 newtons. The value 18000 newtons introduces an extra factor of ten, and 1200 newtons is the mass rather than the force.

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.50 kilograms is moving at 8.0 metres per second. What is its kinetic energy?
options: 2.0 joules
16 joules
32 joules
64 joules
items.explanation: Kinetic energy is one half m v squared, so 0.5 times 0.50 times 64 gives 16 joules. The value 2.0 joules comes from using one half m v, 32 joules from omitting the one half, and 64 joules from squaring the speed alone.

items.stem: A wave has a frequency of 50 hertz and a wavelength of 4.0 metres. What is the speed of the wave?
options: 12.5 metres per second
50 metres per second
4.0 metres per second
200 metres per second
items.explanation: Wave speed is frequency multiplied by wavelength, so 50 times 4.0 gives 200 metres per second. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 12.5, while the other options quote the frequency or the wavelength on their own.

items.stem: How many moles are present in 22.0 grams of carbon dioxide, given that carbon has a relative mass of 12.0 and oxygen 16.0?
options: 1.25 moles
0.440 moles
0.500 moles
2.00 moles
items.explanation: The molar mass of carbon dioxide is 12.0 plus 2 times 16.0, which is 44.0 grams per mole, so moles equals 22.0 divided by 44.0, giving 0.500. The other answers use an incorrect molar mass or divide in the wrong direction.

items.stem: What volume of a 2.00 mole per litre sodium hydroxide solution contains 0.250 moles of solute?
options: 500 millilitres
125 millilitres
250 millilitres
1000 millilitres
items.explanation: Volume equals amount divided by concentration, so 0.250 divided by 2.00 is 0.125 litres, which is 125 millilitres. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 500 millilitres, and the other values ignore one of the quantities.

items.stem: For the equilibrium between nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia with a negative enthalpy change for the forward reaction, what is the immediate effect of cooling a sealed container?
options: The equilibrium shifts to the right, producing more ammonia
The equilibrium shifts to the left, producing more nitrogen and hydrogen
The equilibrium does not move because concentrations are unchanged
The equilibrium shifts right only if a catalyst is added
items.explanation: The forward reaction releases heat, so lowering the temperature favours the exothermic direction and the position of equilibrium moves to the right. A catalyst changes only the rate, and cooling does allow concentrations to change as equilibrium is re-established.

items.stem: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 1 times 10 to the power negative 3 moles per litre. What is the pH of the solution?
items.explanation: pH is the negative base 10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, so the negative log of 10 to the negative 3 is 3. The value 11 is the pOH of the same solution, and 0.001 is the raw concentration rather than a pH.

items.stem: A class measures how temperature affects an enzyme-controlled reaction. The rate rises to an optimum near 37 degrees Celsius and then falls sharply above that temperature. Which explanation best accounts for the fall?
options: All of the substrate had been consumed before higher temperatures were tested
The enzyme denatures, so its active site no longer fits the substrate
The reaction becomes endothermic above 37 degrees Celsius
The concentration of enzyme increases as the temperature rises
items.explanation: Above the optimum, thermal energy disrupts the enzyme's structure so the active site changes shape and no longer binds the substrate, lowering the rate. Substrate depletion would reduce the rate at every temperature, and reactions do not switch to endothermic on heating.

items.stem: A plant is kept under controlled light and its rate of photosynthesis plateaus even though light intensity keeps increasing. What is the most likely explanation for the plateau?
options: Light intensity is still the factor limiting the rate
The plant has stopped using carbon dioxide entirely
The chlorophyll has been permanently bleached by the light
Another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature is limiting
items.explanation: If the rate fails to rise while light keeps increasing, light is no longer the bottleneck, so another requirement such as carbon dioxide supply or temperature has become limiting. The plateau itself shows that the plant is still photosynthesising.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why meiosis, rather than mitosis, must occur in the production of gametes for sexual reproduction?
options: Meiosis produces four identical diploid cells for growth and repair
Meiosis allows the organism to grow larger with each generation
Meiosis halves the chromosome number and adds genetic variation, so fertilisation restores a full set
Mitosis produces gametes that are genetically identical to body cells
items.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and reshuffles alleles through crossing over and independent assortment, so fertilisation can restore a full set with new combinations. Mitosis produces identical body cells for growth, not gametes, and does not halve chromosomes.

items.stem: A rock contains 25 grams of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 1600 years. What mass of that isotope remains after 4800 years?
options: 6.25 grams
3.125 grams
12.5 grams
8.33 grams
items.explanation: 4800 years is three half-lives, so the mass halves three times: 25 to 12.5 to 6.25 to 3.125 grams. The value 12.5 grams corresponds to only one half-life and 6.25 grams to two, so both stop too early.

items.stem: In a region with heavy industrial soot, dark-coloured moths rose from 20 per cent of the population in 1900 to 80 per cent by 1950 while light-coloured moths declined. Which interpretation is best supported by these data?
options: Dark colouring became more common because it conferred a survival advantage in the changed environment
Individual moths darkened their wings in response to soot during their own lifetimes
The total number of moths in the population increased steadily every decade
Light-coloured moths ceased to reproduce at all after the year 1900
items.explanation: A shift in the frequency of an inherited trait shows that dark-coloured moths survived and bred better against the sooted background, so natural selection favoured them. Selection acts on existing variation rather than changing individuals within a lifetime.

items.stem: Two seismograph stations record the same earthquake. The station nearer the epicentre reports a larger ground amplitude and an earlier arrival. Which conclusion is best supported by this evidence?
options: Seismic wave amplitude generally decreases with distance from the epicentre
The more distant station was actually closer to the focus of the quake
Both stations must have recorded the arrival at exactly the same time
The earthquake was centred beneath the more distant station
items.explanation: Seismic waves lose energy as they travel, so amplitude falls and arrival is later at greater distances from the epicentre. Both stations record the same earthquake, so the origin cannot lie beneath the more distant one.

items.stem: Atmospheric carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 400 parts per million recently, while global mean temperature has also risen. Which statement best reflects the scientific interpretation of these data?
options: Because carbon dioxide and temperature rose together, no other factor can have contributed to warming
Higher temperatures caused all of the industrial emissions of carbon dioxide
Because many factors influence climate, the rise in carbon dioxide can have no effect
The rise in carbon dioxide from human activity is a major driver of the warming, alongside other factors
items.explanation: The increase in carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is a major driver of the observed warming and works alongside other influences such as land-use change and natural variability. A correlation does not show that warming caused the emissions or that carbon dioxide has no effect.

items.stem: In the years before 1914 Germany's naval expansion threatened Britain's control of the seas, and Britain responded by laying down more warships of its own. Which feature of the period does this example best illustrate?
options: The success of secret diplomacy in preventing any armed conflict
The complete collapse of the alliance system across Europe
A naval arms race that deepened mutual suspicion between Britain and Germany
The decline of naval power as a factor in international diplomacy
items.explanation: Competitive shipbuilding on both sides is a classic arms race, which bred fear and mistrust and helped create the conditions for war in 1914. The example shows neither successful diplomacy nor the collapse of alliances.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A soldier's letter from Gallipoli describes the landing as chaotic and costly, while an official report from the same day praises the discipline of the troops. How should a historian use these two sources together?
options: Assume the official report is false because its writer was not a soldier
Compare the purpose and audience of each source, recognising both are shaped by context
Use only the soldier's letter, since only a participant can be accurate
Conclude that the landing was neither chaotic nor disciplined
items.explanation: Both are evidence shaped by purpose: a private letter admits hardship while an official report reassures its readers. Reading them for context and intent rather than declaring one false is how historians handle conflicting accounts.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A national price index rises from 110 to 121 over one year. What was the inflation rate for that year, to the nearest whole percent?
options: 9 percent
10 percent
11 percent
21 percent
items.explanation: Inflation is the percentage change in the index, so 121 minus 110 divided by 110, multiplied by 100, gives 10 per cent. Dividing the wrong way gives about 9 per cent, treating the point change as a share of 100 gives 11 per cent, and subtracting 100 from the new index gives 21 per cent.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A student can spend a free Saturday either working a paid shift worth 150 dollars or completing a practice exam she values at 200 dollars of preparation. She chooses the practice exam. What is the opportunity cost of her decision?
options: The 150 dollar shift she did not work
The 200 dollars of value she placed on the exam
The 350 dollar total value of both activities
Nothing, because she gained value from the exam
items.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone, which here is the paid shift she gave up. The value of the chosen option or the sum of both options is never the cost of deciding between them.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A city has 500000 residents, gains 5000 people a year from natural increase and 10000 a year through net migration. What is its annual population growth rate?
options: 1 percent
2 percent
3 percent
0.3 percent
items.explanation: Total annual increase is 5000 plus 10000, which is 15000 people, and 15000 divided by 500000 gives 3 per cent. Counting only natural increase gives 1 per cent, counting only migration gives 2 per cent, and 0.3 per cent misplaces the decimal point.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A weather station records 950 millimetres of rain in summer and under 10 millimetres in winter, with hot summers and mild winters. Which climate type best matches this pattern?
options: Mediterranean, with wet winters and dry summers
Tropical savanna, with a wet summer and a dry winter
Humid continental, with cold winters and rain all year
Polar, with frozen conditions throughout the year
items.explanation: Hot wet summers with a pronounced dry winter match the tropical savanna climate of northern Australia. A Mediterranean climate has the reverse seasonal pattern, wet winters and dry summers, and the other two options require cold or frozen conditions.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: Under the Australian Constitution, which statement correctly describes the relationship between Parliament, the Executive and the Judiciary?
options: Parliament makes laws, the Executive administers them, and the Judiciary interprets them
The Judiciary makes laws that the Executive must then overturn
The Executive is chosen by the Judiciary and answers only to the courts
Parliament and the Judiciary are the same body operating under two names
items.explanation: The separation of powers assigns legislation to Parliament, administration to the Executive, and interpretation and review to the Judiciary. The other options invert or collapse roles that the Constitution keeps distinct.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: What is required before a proposed amendment to the Australian Constitution is approved at a referendum?
options: A majority of voters across the nation only
A majority of voters in the states only, whatever the national result
A two-thirds majority of both Houses of Parliament
A majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in at least four of the six states
items.explanation: Section 128 requires a double majority: more than half the national vote and more than half the votes in at least four of the six states. Either majority alone fails, and Parliament cannot alter the Constitution by ordinary vote.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: In a House of Representatives election conducted by preferential voting, no candidate reaches 50 per cent of first-preference votes. What happens next?
options: The election is cancelled and the whole seat is held again
The candidate with the fewest first preferences is excluded and their ballot papers flow to the next choice
The candidate with the most first preferences wins outright despite falling short of 50 per cent
All ballot papers are recounted by hand before any preferences are examined
items.explanation: Preferential voting requires a majority of formal votes, so the lowest candidate is excluded and second preferences are distributed until one candidate passes 50 per cent. A plurality alone does not win the seat and the election is not voided.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: Which development most directly encouraged the Australian colonies to federate and form the Commonwealth in 1901?
options: The practical need to remove colonial tariff barriers and share defence and immigration policy
A requirement imposed by Britain that the colonies must unite by 1901
The defeat of every colony by foreign invasion during the 1890s
The collapse of the colonial parliaments, which left no alternative government
items.explanation: Disagreeing colonies saw clear gains in removing internal tariffs and coordinating defence, immigration and railway policy, which drove the 1890s conventions and the 1901 Constitution. Britain did not compel union and no invasion occurred.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A severe frost destroys part of a citrus crop while consumer incomes are unchanged. What is the most likely immediate effect in the market for orange juice?
options: Both supply and demand shift right, leaving the price unchanged
Demand shifts left, so the equilibrium price falls
Supply shifts right, so the equilibrium price falls
Supply shifts left, so the equilibrium price rises and quantity falls
items.explanation: A destroyed crop reduces quantity supplied at every price, shifting supply left against an unchanged demand curve, which raises price and lowers quantity traded. Demand does not move and supply does not shift right when production is lost.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: One historian explains the Cold War mainly through Soviet expansion, while another stresses Western containment and economic pressure. How should a student evaluate these competing interpretations?
options: Accept the first account because that historian is the more famous writer
Reject both accounts because no historian can interpret the Cold War accurately
Weigh the evidence each interpretation cites and consider whether several factors combined to cause the events
Choose whichever interpretation best matches the student's own political views
items.explanation: Rival interpretations are judged against the evidence each cites, and the strongest explanations usually combine several causes rather than selecting one. Choosing by reputation or preference is not historical method, and discarding both ignores the available evidence.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: The High Court's Mabo decision recognised that native title could survive British settlement in Australia. What was the most significant immediate consequence of that decision?
options: It overturned the doctrine of terra nullius and allowed native title where it had not been extinguished
It granted unrestricted ownership of all Australian land to Indigenous Australians
It ended the High Court's power to interpret the Constitution
It made further native title claims impossible after 1992
items.explanation: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) rejected terra nullius and confirmed that native title can persist where it has not been clearly extinguished, leading to the Native Title Act 1993. It granted no blanket ownership and left the Court's role intact.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: On a map with a scale of 1 to 50000, two towns are 7.5 centimetres apart. What is the actual straight-line distance between them?
options: 1.5 kilometres
15 kilometres
375 kilometres
3.75 kilometres
items.explanation: At a scale of 1 to 50000 each centimetre stands for 50000 centimetres, so 7.5 centimetres represents 375000 centimetres, which converts to 3.75 kilometres. The other answers convert the scale or the units incorrectly.
items.reference: Australian Senior Secondary Curriculum - Humanities and Social Sciences

items.stem: A factory's production sends smoke over neighbouring homes, and the factory pays none of the health costs that neighbours suffer. How would an economist describe this situation?
options: A public good, because the smoke is available to everyone
A negative externality, because costs fall on third parties outside the transaction
A positive externality, because the smoke shows the factory is operating
A free rider problem, because neighbours refuse to pay for clean air
items.explanation: Costs imposed on people who are neither buyers nor sellers of the product are negative externalities, and the standard response is regulation or a Pigouvian tax. A public good is non-excludable and non-rival, and the smoke described is a cost rather than a benefit.
